title: Multiple Linear Regression — I
subtitle: A visual guide to least squares, model fit, inference, and special explanatory variables

sections.title: From multivariate data to a fitted plane
items: Collect \(n\) observations with \(k\) explanatory variables and one response: \((x_{i1},\ldots,x_{ik},y_i)\).
Inspect variables individually; use transformations such as LNFACE and LNINCOME when skewness and nonlinear patterns suggest them.
Use scatterplot matrices and correlation matrices to summarize pairwise relationships.

sections.title: Least squares objective
sections.value: Determine the coefficients that minimize the sum of squared differences between observed and fitted responses.
sections.label: Equation (3.1)

sections.title: Matrix solution and estimator properties
items: Normal equations vs solution: \(\mathbf X'\mathbf X\mathbf b=\mathbf X'\mathbf y\) vs \(\mathbf b=(\mathbf X'\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf X'\mathbf y\)
Unbiasedness vs precision: \(\mathrm E\mathbf b=\boldsymbol\beta\) vs \(\mathrm{Var}\mathbf b=\sigma^2(\mathbf X'\mathbf X)^{-1}\)
F1–F4 vs F1–F5: Gauss–Markov gives minimum-variance unbiased linear estimation vs normality additionally gives a normal distribution for \(\mathbf b\)

sections.label: Regression of LNFACE on EDUCATION, NUMHH, and LNINCOME; Table 3.3

sections.title: Goodness-of-fit measures
sections.label: \(R^2\) is the proportion of variability explained; \(s\) is the residual standard deviation

sections.title: Test whether one coefficient matters
items: Compute \(se(b_j)\) from \(s\) and the corresponding diagonal element of \((\mathbf X'\mathbf X)^{-1}\).
Reject \(H_0\) when \u007c\(t(b_j)\)\u007c exceeds the appropriate \(t\)-critical value; as a rule of thumb at 5%, a magnitude above two indicates importance.

sections.title: Extending the linear model
items: Binary variable vs continuous variable: a binary coefficient compares the alternative level with its base level; a continuous coefficient is an expected change per unit change, holding other variables fixed.
Transformation vs nonlinear regression function: \(x, x^2,\ldots,x^p\) or \(\ln x\) can be explanatory variables while the model remains linear in its parameters.
Interaction vs additive effects: with \(x_3=x_1x_2\), \(\partial\mathrm E y/\partial x_1=\beta_1+\beta_3x_2\), so the effect of one variable depends on the other.
Pairwise correlation vs partial correlation: an added variable plot controls for other explanatory variables and can reveal a relationship different from the unadjusted correlation.
